p: Wednesday, January 31, 2063. 4:50 AM. He'd slept three hours and woken at the minute he'd have woken for a log, and there wasn't one, so he made the coffee anyway and listened to the machine sigh.

The results page was on the kitchen table where he'd left it at midnight, printed, because he'd wanted it on paper. CLOSE 3: 12 MILLISECONDS. MET. Under it, in the board's capitals, the line that had been written into the rules in January and kept: IT PASSES C1. IT DOESN'T EXPLAIN THE VALVE.

The board's notice had posted at 9:40 the night before, two lines. ITEM 1: THE BOARD WILL SIT ON THE RESULT THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 1, AT 0900. THE CONSENT PASS FOLLOWS THE SAME EVENING. Hana had texted at 3:12, which meant she hadn't gone home either. Still here. Not a finding. Don't ask me till 8.

Mars was a little over eleven minutes away by light. On the station it would be late afternoon, and somebody in the galley would still have the results page up on the big screen, because Ada had said in a log once that they kept things up until somebody on Earth told them what they meant.

On the counter by the door the envelope to Ruth was under his keys, where it had been since February of last year. The photocopy was still in it, with STILL ASKING beside the third row in Nell's blue ink, and it was still unsealed.

He got the gas bill out of the drawer by the phone charger, the drawer with Grace's reading glasses in it, folded, on top of the takeout menus. The bill had gone soft as cloth along its creases. Minus seventeen, in his own hand from January of 2061. Minus nine under it. The part number. He wrote 12 under all of it, and then didn't know what to write after it, and put the bill back.

Twenty miles east, over the high bay doors, the clock said 18. Eighteen days to the planned burn. Thirty two to the last day the window would allow. Then it would close, and the next one was twenty six months away, and it wouldn't be for them.
Ruth's Console Log, page fifteen: The blank page.
Ruth's console log. Petrel. After. Page 15.

That's the whole page. Nothing on it. I put a fresh sheet in the binder one morning in the summer of 2036, after the rule was in the book and the investigation board's report had gone to the printer, and I sat at this table and couldn't think of a thing to write on it. I've moved that page from binder to binder for twenty six years. It's the only page I never mailed you.
I'll write one more line on it before I give it away. I don't know yet what it'll say. I think I'll know when I hear the poll.

This chapter is about the end of a project, which is the part people skip. The Standard calls it the Closing Focus Area, in 4.5.5, and describes it as the work of formally completing a project, a phase, or a contract, or of ending one early when that's the best thing left to do. It says the point is to close things out properly and hand them to operations in a way that still meets the project's purpose, and that closing includes checking the outputs, the outcomes, and the benefits. Not only the outputs. A ship that leaves on time is an output. Air at Ares Station is the reason anybody built it.

So this chapter covers the last decision, the go/no-go with a risk still in it, and then everything after: handing the work over, closing the contracts, turning lessons into rules, measuring a benefit that outlives you, letting people go well, and deciding what goes in the archive and what belongs to somebody.

How the exam asks it. Closing questions reward the answer that finishes the work formally: acceptance, transition, contracts, lessons, release, archive. "The team moved on" and "it went live" are not closure.
A go/no-go with a known residual risk is the hardest kind, because everybody in the room has already done the honest work and the result still isn't zero. Three things are worth holding onto.

First, accepting a risk doesn't remove it. When the right authority accepts a residual risk in writing, with the consent of the people exposed to it, the risk is still there on the day. What's changed is that the people who decided can say what they decided on. Read it out, on the day, so everyone answering the poll answers on the same facts.

Second, every voice on a poll is its own voice. Each station answers for its own system, and each one can say hold and say why. When somebody pauses, the person running the poll asks them to say again. A pause is information. I heard one in 2035 and didn't ask, and I've told you what that cost.

Third, a hold is an answer. The Standard's section on life cycles, 4.1, lists what can come out of a gate: go on, go on with changes, stay in the phase, repeat it, park it for a while, or end it. A hold is staying put, and it's on that list for a reason. A program that can't say no on the day has already said yes to everything.
And your own answer, if you have one on the poll, is what the record supports, not what the room needs. You can be sorry about it afterward. You can't be vague about it at the time.

How the exam asks it. At a final go/no-go, the best answer validates readiness against the agreed criteria and record, gives each participant their own voice, and treats a hold as a valid outcome. Answering go to protect a date is the distractor.

The Guide covers closing in Close Project or Phase, section 2.1.6.9, and it's worth reading slowly. It says the process applies to successful and unsuccessful projects alike, and to phases, releases, iterations, and contracts. Its benefits are archiving the information, completing the planned work, and releasing the organization's resources, and it includes confirming how far the value was actually achieved.

For a predictive project it lists the steps. Make sure the deliverables were formally accepted. Make sure there's a plan to keep the value going once the work moves to operations. Transfer the results to the next phase or to operations. And it says something people forget: identify the outstanding risks and either have them accepted or transfer them to operations. A risk doesn't close because the project does. It gets a new owner, by name, who knows they have it.

The exam outline's R10 puts the test in four words: validate readiness for transition. The receiving team says it's ready, against criteria it agreed, before the hand off, not after. Ask the person who'll run the thing on Monday whether they're ready, and listen to how they say it.

How the exam asks it. Before handover, confirm formal acceptance and the receiving team's readiness against agreed criteria, and transfer open risks to named owners. Handing over on the scheduled date regardless is wrong.

A contract closes too, and it has its own list in the same section. Confirm formal acceptance of the supplier's work. Finalize any open claims, guarantees, and warranties. Update the records to show the final results. Make sure every invoice due is paid. Archive what matters for future use. Settle any dispute, or send it to whoever settles disputes. The Guide also describes a procurement audit, in section 5, as a structured review of the whole procurement for completeness, accuracy, and effectiveness, with what it finds going to both sides.

Two things make that list honest instead of administrative. Pay what's owed, on time, whatever you'd like to have done differently; holding money back as leverage at the end isn't negotiating in good faith, which the Code asks of us in 3.3.1. And put the whole story in the record, including what the supplier got right. If a supplier warned you and you didn't listen, the record has to say so, or the next buyer will make your mistake with your file open in front of them.

How the exam asks it. At contract closeout: formal acceptance, claims and invoices settled, records updated, history archived. Withholding payment owed, or closing on paperwork while leaving out what was learned, are distractors.

The Guide's lessons learned register, in section 4, is started early and kept up all the way through, and at the end of a project it moves into the organization's lessons learned repository. That's necessary. It isn't enough. A lesson in a repository is a lesson somebody might read.

The same closing section asks you for something better: collect suggestions for improving the organization's policies and procedures, and forward them to the unit that owns them. The outline's B6 says the same thing in its own words: use lessons learned, make sure improvement processes are updated, update the organization's process assets. Process assets are the rules, templates, and procedures the next team inherits. If your lesson doesn't change one of them, the next team inherits the old one.

So route each lesson that should change something to the office that owns the thing it should change, with the evidence and a proposed change, and make sure somebody there has their name on it. And keep blame out of it. A lessons session that becomes a search for who did it teaches everyone to hide the next one, and the Code's 5.2.5 asks us to make it safe to tell the truth.

In agile closing, the Guide puts the same work in retrospectives: what happened, what we'd change, what risks still need an owner. Different meeting, same rule. A lesson has to land somewhere it'll be acted on.

How the exam asks it. For lessons at closure, the best answer sends each improvement to the owner of the policy or procedure, with evidence and a proposal, and archives the register. Filing it without action, or turning it into blame, are wrong.

Most projects close before their benefit has happened. A ship arrives months after its program ends. A clinic's new system pays off in a year of appointments. That's normal, and the Guide plans for it.

The benefits management plan, in section 4, names a benefits owner, the person accountable for monitoring, recording, and reporting what's actually realized over the plan's timeframe. At closing, that plan gets handed to its owner formally, with somebody named to receive her reports after the project is gone. Otherwise the benefit is measured faithfully and read by nobody.

The final report, in the same section, says how to tell the truth about it. It summarizes the project against its objectives and criteria, with the evidence that they were met. And if the benefits aren't met at close, it says how far they've been achieved and gives an estimate of when the rest will be. A report that says complete, successful, and nothing about the reason for the project has told the reader about the paperwork.

How the exam asks it. When benefits come after closure, the right answer hands measurement to a named owner with a receiver and reviews, and the final report states the degree achieved so far. Declaring the benefit delivered at handover is the distractor.

The closing section's list includes reassigning or releasing the project's people. Do it on the dates you told them. The Code's 2.2.3 is short: we do what we say we'll do. Keeping people past a promised release just in case costs them real things, jobs and moves and plans, for a risk a handover and an on call list would cover.

Release them well. Every piece of their open work goes to a named person who agrees to take it. And thank them in a way that fits them. The Guide's section on recognition says rewards land best when they're tailored to the people and the culture, that intangible rewards can matter as much as money, and that recognition belongs all through a project, not only at the end. In the Resources domain's tailoring section it adds celebrating success, so the team can see what it did.

Ask people how they'd like to be thanked. The answer is usually smaller than the plan. A morning, a thermos, the right person in the room. Then, if someone's ready for a bigger job, don't hold them back to finish yours. Ask what they want, free them on a date that works, and tell the next organization honestly what they can do.

How the exam asks it. Release team members on committed dates with a proper handover, and recognize them in ways they value. Holding people "just in case" or deferring thanks until benefits are confirmed are distractors.

The closing section asks you twice to archive: the project's information for future use, and each contract's records. Archive completely. The next team needs the reasoning behind your criteria, the consents, the data that were inconvenient, and the run sheets, more than it needs the polished report. Organize it so somebody can find things, and stop there.

Archive only what's yours to archive. The Code's 3.3.4 asks us to respect the property rights of others, and it says plainly that property includes documents and data. A person's own notes, however useful they were to your project, go into an organization's archive only if that person agrees. Ask them. If they say no, that's the answer. Some knowledge is meant to be handed to a person, not filed.
How the exam asks it. Archive project records completely and accessibly, and include another person's private material only with their consent.

The Guide says Close Project or Phase applies to unsuccessful projects too, and it asks for procedures to investigate and document why a project was ended before completion. The Standard's Closing Focus Area says the same, that closing can mean ending a project early when that's the best way left to limit the loss.

Close a failed project as carefully as a good one. More carefully. Accept what can be accepted. Hand over what can be used. Close the contracts honestly. Write down why, without blame and without softening it, and send the lessons to the people who own the rules. Release people on time and thank them anyway, because they worked as hard on the thing that didn't work. The next attempt is built from what you write down now.
How the exam asks it. A cancelled or failed project still gets formal closure: records, contracts, lessons, release, and a documented reason. Simply stopping work is wrong.

I've given you fourteen pages, one at a time, in order, and I'd like to say why it was in order. You can't skip to the end of a thing like the Petrel. You have to go through it the way it happened, or you take the wrong lesson from it. I took a few wrong ones myself before I got the right ones.

Here's the right one, as short as I can make it. You won't always get to know. I didn't get to know what was in a second on my poll. You won't get to know about a Thursday in Arizona. Not knowing doesn't excuse anybody from deciding. It means you decide on what's in front of you, out loud, with the people who'll live with it, and then you carry the rest. You don't put it down. You learn how to carry it without dropping anything else.
The binder's going to somebody now. I'll write the last line before I give it to him.
How the exam asks it. When in doubt at the end: formal acceptance, an honest handover, contracts closed, lessons routed, people released and thanked, records archived, and the benefit given an owner.

Thursday, February 1. 9:00 AM. The hearing room on the fourth floor, with the same coffee and a fuller gallery. Frances Odum was in the third row with the binder on her knees. Greaves had his camera at the back. Hale sat in the front row with her coat folded on the chair beside her, which for Hale meant she expected to stay.

On the screen beside the bench, from Halcyon's habitat module, the four of them were in a row against the wall with their feet in loops, and Haddad had pointed the camera so a pressure gauge showed in the corner of the frame. The relay put a second and a bit between a question and its answer. After two years of Mars it felt like being in the same room.

Esther Quayle called item one at 9:01 and set the kitchen timer. The criteria were met. This board wrote down in January what that makes the workaround and what it doesn't. Today we decide. Mr. Okafor, the program first.

On Wednesday Hana had come in at 8:02 with a page she'd printed at 7:40, and she'd let him read it in the hall. At 6:50 on Wednesday morning, after a soak as long as the one on orbit, the second test article in Building 6 had rippled on its third close at 13 milliseconds, past the ground limit for the first time in its life, at 3,140 cycles. The borescope showed the polished ring on its seat wider than it had been at 2,400. Then she'd written the line she'd refused to write for fourteen months. FINDING: SEAT WEAR. THE 2058 LOT'S SEAT INSERTS POLISH A RING UNDER COLD CYCLING, AND AFTER A SOAK THE POPPET HANGS ON IT AT THE THIRD CLOSE. MOIV-1 AND THIS ARTICLE HAVE 2058 INSERTS. THE REPLACEMENT VALVE HAS A 2062 INSERT AND ELEVEN CYCLES ON IT. She'd signed it. It had taken two years of closure history, back to the month he'd reopened AR 2207, and the extra cold shifts in Building 6 that the declared reserve had paid for in the fall.

Quinn had the screen. Hale had asked him at the elevator, quietly, whether the program was going to ask for acceptance. Garrett had asked the same thing by text, less quietly. Ruth was second from the left on the bench with the green pen clipped in its pocket, and she hadn't looked at the program's table yet.
A. Lead with close three sitting above the ground limit, so the board sees the risk plainly and orders the spacewalk before anyone talks it down.
B. Give the board the results and both options in full, and leave the recommendation out, so the program can't be seen to lean on the decision.
C. Ask the board to accept the workaround today, since all six criteria are met and Rule A is exactly what everybody agreed to in January.
D. Show the board every value as measured, against both limits, with what's unexplained, each option with its risks and dates, and his recommendation.

He takes thirty minutes, and Quinn keeps the slides plain. Close three on the screen with two lines through it, fifteen in red and ten in gray, and the ripple starting 2 milliseconds after lift. What it passes and what it doesn't explain. The root cause as it stood at eight that morning, in Hana's words, read out with her name on them. Revision C against D, still unexplained. Each option with its residual risk, its crew time, and the date after which it stops being possible. Then the program's recommendation, which he says is a recommendation, and which takes him one sentence, because he wrote it at four in the morning and has been crossing words out of it since. The chair thanks him and sets the timer again.

That's a go. Evaluate status honestly at a gate: every measurement against its limits, what's known and unknown, the options with their risks and deadlines, and a recommendation stated as one. Then the authority decides on the same picture you have.
4:10 PM. The decision posted while he was still in the hall outside the hearing room. Quinn read it on her phone and turned it so he could see, and kept her other hand flat on the windowsill.

INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD DECISION ITEM 1 FEBRUARY 1, 2063, 1610. THE CRITERIA WERE MET. THE CAUSE IS NOW KNOWN TO THIS BOARD'S SATISFACTION: SEAT WEAR (TALLGRASS FINDING OF JANUARY 31, BUILDING 6).. MOIV-1 WILL BE REPLACED BY SPACEWALK WITH THE VALVE FLOWN ON JANUARY 9. SPACEWALKS SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 3, AND TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 6. RETEST FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 16, ON THE SAME SIX CRITERIA, AFTER THE SAME SOAK.. THE CR 62-311 WORKAROUND STAYS LOADED AS A SECOND BARRIER.. THE BOARD ACCEPTS THE RESIDUAL RISK OF THE SPACEWALKS AND OF THE NEW VALVE, SUBJECT TO THE WRITTEN CONSENT OF EACH MEMBER OF THE CREW, ASKED TONIGHT.. VOTE 6 TO 0.. E. QUAYLE, CHAIR

The consent pass was at seven, on the loop, ninety minutes on Lorna's timeline, with the chair asking each of the four separately on a private channel. Tonight each of them would be asked whether they'd go outside on a loaded stage and change a valve, and then fly on the new one.

By 6:20 three people had ideas about how it should open. Hale wanted two minutes first. They're about to hear what the board did with their lives. Before they answer, somebody should tell them what eleven governments put in for them. It's true, and they've never heard it from us. Garrett wanted Hana to brief the engineering before anyone said anything else, so the crew wouldn't get it wrong. Quinn had the program's own summary of the ruling on one page, if Sam wanted it read.
At 6:31 a message came down from Haddad, one line. We have the data. We've read it twice. Who talks first?
A. Ask that the crew speak first, each in their own words and order, with the data already uplinked and nobody briefing them beforehand.
B. Let Haddad hear it first and decide how to put it to her crew, since she knows them best, and keep everybody else off the loop for it.
C. Open with the program's one page summary of the ruling and the data, so each crew member hears it in context before the chair asks.
D. Open the pass with Hale's statement on what the partners put in, so the crew hears the stakes before anyone asks them anything at all.

The chair says yes before Hale can get her coat off the chair. The data went up at five. At seven the chair takes each of them on a private channel, in the order they chose, and nobody else is on any of them. Dr. Rao starts, with what the four of them have slept and eaten since Monday, because a doctor ought to say that out loud before people answer questions like these. Echeverría asks one question about MOIV-2, and page nine of the data answers it. Brandvold reads off an index card she wrote out twice, and stops once to fix a word. Haddad goes last. Her answer's one sentence long. The clerk types each answer as it's said, and on the ground nobody says a thing till they're done.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Lead by representing the team's voice, not speaking over it: the people who carry the risk get the data first, speak first in their own words, and nobody frames it for them. That's what makes what they say worth recording.
Tuesday, February 6. 6:30 AM. The program room at Watkins. Over the high bay doors across the road, the clock said 12.

Haddad and Echeverría had done the first spacewalk on Saturday in six hours and forty minutes. The second was today at 9:10, with the old valve coming off and the new one going on, and the whole building was going to watch it, so Quinn had put this meeting before.
Okonkwo's packet had come in overnight, one way a little under eleven minutes and a day late, the way her answers always came.

ARES STATION BREATHER OPERATIONS ENGINEERING PACKET 409 SOL 4253. 1. UNDERSTOOD AS: THE PROGRAM CLOSES AFTER THE HAND OFF. THE BENEFIT STARTS WHEN THE BREATHER DOES, MONTHS LATER. WHO ON EARTH READS MY LINE ONE WHEN THERE IS NO PROGRAM?. 2. BAY D ON THE MAIN LOOP, SOL 4232 TO 4251, MEASURED AGAINST THE PROJECTED QUARTER DAY. TABLE ATTACHED. WE ARE NOT ROUNDING IT.. 3. IF THE ANSWER TO 1 IS NOBODY, PLEASE SAY SO. WE WILL MEASURE ANYWAY. WE WOULD LIKE TO BE READ.. C. OKONKWO

Quinn had the program's closeout plan on the screen beside it. The program office closed on March 30. After that, nothing in it said who would receive a benefit report from Mars, or what they'd do with one.

Hale's office had a view, in an email from the night before: the benefit was the program's headline, and the final report should state it as delivered on arrival. Hollis's office had offered to carry it in the director's weekly, beside the margin. The ARA's mission assurance office said its model could compute a benefit from Earth after closure, the way it had in January.
A. Let Hollis's office carry the benefit in the director's weekly report, since it already sends the station's margin to the ARA every Monday.
B. Report the benefit as delivered on arrival in the final report, since the measuring after that is the station's own business, not the program's.
C. Keep two people in the program office until the ninety sols are over, so the program itself can confirm the benefit it was built for.
D. Hand the plan to Okonkwo formally, name who on Earth receives her reports after the program closes, and set reviews that run past closure.

He writes it with Quinn and Okonkwo across two packets, because the station answers a day later. The plan goes to her by name, signed by Hale as sponsor. After March 30, Okonkwo's weekly line one goes to the ARA's mission assurance office, which accepts it in writing, with a copy to the board for as long as the board sits on Halcyon. Reviews at thirty, sixty, and ninety sols after the Breather starts, and one more at a year. Two sols of falling reserve in a row still triggers a call with Lorna's team. Okonkwo's reply has a line at the bottom. Understood as: somebody will read it.

Exactly right. Before the project closes, hand the benefits plan to its owner formally, with a named receiving authority, metrics, and review dates that run past the end. That's how value measured after closure still gets measured and heard.

Monday, February 12. 8:00 AM. Flight control. Lorna had the hand off on her whiteboard as a single line with a box at the end. DEPARTURE PLUS 24 MON FEB 19 0906. She'd drawn the box in December and hadn't touched it since.

At eight she wanted one thing she didn't have. The program's lessons register. Not the report you'll write in March. The register, this week. My people are taking a ship that's had two years of things go wrong on it, and I'd like to know which of them are still in it.

It was in Quinn's folder: four hundred and twelve entries since January of 2061, some a line long and some a page, in four people's handwriting and two databases. Thirty of them were Wendell's, in his capitals, taken down by Quinn at his kitchen table in Byers.

Garrett had stopped by on his way to the airport. Send her the final report when it's done. Half that register is raw, and some of it's people being angry at two in the morning. Nobody should be flying a ship on that. Hale's office had suggested sending only the entries marked closed.
A. Send Lorna's team the whole register this morning, all four hundred and twelve entries, so they have every lesson the program ever logged.
B. Send Lorna the final lessons report after closure, when every lesson is complete, so her team gets a finished document and not a raw register.
C. Walk Lorna's team through the register now, flag the lessons that touch flying the ship, and give each an owner who accepts it.
D. Give Lorna only the lessons from work that went well, since her team takes over a working ship and doesn't need two years of old mistakes.

They do it that afternoon and Tuesday morning, Quinn and two of Lorna's controllers and Hana, entry by entry. Of the four hundred and twelve, sixty one touch flying the ship. Each of those gets a line in flight operations' own book with a name beside it, and the controller whose name it is reads it back. Entry 288, the poll and the pause, goes to the lead flight controller. Entry 301, the ripple on the third close after a soak, goes to Lorna's propulsion officer, who asks for the ground runs and the run sheets the same day. The harness revision, C against D, goes to him too, as open. The rest go to the ARA's repository with the program's name on them. Lorna signs the last page and writes under it, in capitals, RECEIVED, NOT JUST SENT.

That's a go. Use lessons learned where they'll be used: review them with the receiving team, pick out the ones that bear on their work, and get each one an owner who accepts it. A lesson handed over without an owner is a file.
Saturday, February 17. 5:40 AM. The kitchen in Aurora, with the coffee maker going. One way nine minutes and thirty five seconds, and shorter every morning.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4265. One way, 9 minutes 35 seconds. Margin, 233 days. Hi, Dad. Log sixty five. Sol 4265. Launch eve. Yours and ours. Malik says it's the first holiday the station's ever had that nobody voted on, and he's made a banner, and it's spelled right, which I checked. The retest. We watched it in the galley yesterday with the numbers coming up a close at a time. Close three, under one millisecond. Okonkwo put her hand flat on the table, and then she laughed, which I've never heard her do before noon. A worn seat. Hana Iwasaki found it in a test article you funded when everybody said there wasn't money. I'd like to meet her. I'd like to meet the article. You haven't done the voice once. I noticed. Don't start tomorrow. Bay D's beating Pilar's line by a hair. We're not counting the hair. Mine's 233. Okonkwo's 240. Arrival's day 201. Plus thirty two. Plus thirty nine. Mom's watch says it'll be half past five there when you watch this. I'll be asleep when you burn, nine and a half minutes behind it. I'm going to try, anyway. Log sixty five. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on her face at the word voice, and left it there while the coffee went cold.
That evening at 7:14, in Golden, Ruth watched a pass she'd worked out on a pad. He didn't know that yet.

At 7:30 he sat down at the kitchen table, in his own chair, and pressed record. In the morning she'd be asleep when the burn started, and whatever he said tonight would be the last thing she heard from him before she knew.
A. Tell her the ruling, what's still unknown, what each answer tomorrow means for the station, and what it's like for him to wait for it.
B. Tell her the board's ruling and the data in full, and leave out what he feels about it, so that the log stays about the ship and not about him.
C. Tell her the ship is going and everything's fine, since tomorrow is the burn and the last thing she hears tonight shouldn't be him worrying.
D. Send her nothing until after the burn, so that she gets one log with the answer in it, not one more night of waiting along with him.

It takes him two tries. He tells her what the board decided and why, what nobody knows yet, and what each answer in the morning would mean for her, for Okonkwo's plant, and for Bay D. Then he tells her he's going to sit at the propulsion end of the room so he can see Hana's screen, and that he's scared in the plain way. Then he tells her the other thing. At the Cape I said your mother would never have let you go. It wasn't true. I was scared, and I used her because she couldn't argue. She'd have driven you to the bus. He doesn't do the voice. He sends it at 8:40 and turns the tablet over, and the coffee maker, which he'd forgotten to switch off, sighs.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Keep the shared vision honest with the people the work is for: what's decided, what's unknown, what each outcome means for them, and enough of yourself that they know it's you talking.

Sunday, February 18. 5:50 AM. Flight control at Watkins, with the wind sock straight out toward Kansas and the parking lot full in the dark. Over the high bay doors across the road, the clock said 0. Somebody had taped a sheet of paper under it that said WE KNOW.

Lorna had set two chairs at the back of the room by the coffee, with names on index cards. One said CALDER and the other said PRICE. Ruth was in hers by six, in the gray cardigan, with the green pen and the green cloth binder on her knees, which she'd never brought anywhere before. Wendell came in at 6:20 with his canvas jacket on and page twelve in his shirt pocket, behind the doctor's note, and sat down beside her. If they said anything to each other, Sam didn't see it.

The retest had run on Friday at 2 PM after a twenty two hour soak, on a valve that had gone up with eleven cycles on it. Five closes. Close three under one millisecond, pressure confirming closed at 29 milliseconds, no ripple. Both blind readers had written the same thing beside every close, and then, because they'd been told to write what they saw, the number.

Garrett had texted at 5:12. Whatever you say, say it like you mean it. Hale was in the front row in her coat. Greaves's feed was carrying flight control's own loop and nothing else. Ignition was at 9:06.
At 8:40 Quinn called the poll. Halcyon departure, final poll. Answer go or no go, or hold and say why. Propulsion.
At the propulsion console Arlo said, Prop is and stopped.
Quinn didn't move on. Prop, say again your status.

Arlo had a hand on page four of the procedure. Question. MOIV-1 body temperature's a degree and a half over the soak model. At her desk Hana had it already, and she answered without looking up. Sun angle. It's on page four, bottom. Inside the model's band. Arlo found the line with his finger. Copy. Prop is go.
In the back row Ruth uncapped the green pen.
Guidance, go. Flight software, go. Communications, go. The range, go. Lorna, for flight operations, go. From orbit Haddad, for the crew, said Halcyon is go, flat and clear.
Then Quinn looked at the last line on her sheet, the one that said PROGRAM, with a box beside it for a signature. Program.
The pen was in the left inside pocket of his jacket, where the jet's forms had gone in Arizona. He could feel it there without touching it.
A. Answer go for the program, since every criterion was met, and attach the whole record to the poll book in writing for anyone who wants to read it.
B. Answer go to hold the date, since the window and the colony both turn on today, and put the open items in the program's report next week.
C. Ask the chair to answer for the program as well as the board, since the risk is the board's to accept and two answers could confuse the loop.
D. Read the record onto the loop first, every value as measured, every open item, the board's terms and the crew's word, then answer what it supports.

Hold for ninety seconds, Quinn. She gives them to him. He reads it the way the board's page reads, flat and in order, without a word of his own in it: the values as measured, what passes and what's still unexplained, the board's terms, the crew's word, the open items and who owns each one. Then he gives the program's answer, the one the record supports, and nothing else, and signs under it with the pen from the left inside pocket. In the back row Ruth writes one line in green and closes the binder on it.

Exactly right. At the final go/no-go, validate readiness against the record, out loud, so everyone on the loop answers on the same facts. Then give the answer the evidence supports and own it. The criteria were written to make this moment a reading, not a feeling.

Sunday, February 18. 9:06 AM. Ignition. Halcyon's departure stage lit over the Pacific, and on the big screen the numbers began to move the way they'd moved in four hundred sims. Nine and a half minutes later the galley on Ares Station saw it too.

9:24. Cutoff command. On Hana's screen MOIV-1's two position channels went to closed together and stayed there, and the pressure downstream said closed at 29 milliseconds. The room didn't clap until Lorna said, Halcyon, Watkins. Clean cutoff. You're on your way. Then it did, once, and stopped, because the hand off was still twenty four hours away.

Wednesday, February 21. 10:00 AM. Pueblo. Aldergrove's conference room had the same view of the steel mill it had in December of 2061, and Peg had brought two coffees and drunk the first one in the parking lot.

The contract had four things left in it: formal acceptance of both valves, the last of the task order that had come out of the November 2061 claim, the final invoices, and the record. Nell had called him on Thursday afternoon, as she'd done most Thursdays for a year, to say the cold data said nothing new.
Garrett had sent his view from the plane. Hold their last payment until somebody can tell me whose valve that was. It's the only lever we've got left.
Nell came in last, with her father's badge on its frayed lanyard and a fat brown folder, and put the folder on the table and didn't say what was in it.
A. Close the contract on paperwork alone, acceptance and invoices and a mutual release, and keep the valve's history in Tallgrass's own files.
B. Hold Aldergrove's last payment as leverage until the valve's behavior is settled, since money is the only hold left on the supplier.
C. Confirm acceptance, settle every claim and invoice, and write the valve's whole history into the record, 2034 warning included.
D. Close it out in full with a letter of thanks to Nell, and leave the 2034 data and her father's letters out of the record, as a courtesy.

It takes the morning. Peg reads each clause aloud and Aldergrove's controller ticks it. Both valves accepted, with what each one did in service written beside it. The task order closed at its final cost and paid within the month. The release signed both ways. Then the record, which takes longer, because Sam asks for it to start in 2034: the rev C cold cycle data with the third row boxed and CYCLE 3 AFTER SO in the margin, Emmett Garrity's request of April 2035 for three weeks, the termination for default and the 2039 ruling that it wasn't one, and every June letter since, by date. Peg writes one line at the top of the closeout in her own words. The supplier asked. It's in here. Nell takes her father's badge off its lanyard and lays it on the folder, and then picks it back up. Not yet, she says.

That's a go. Close a contract completely: formal acceptance, claims and invoices settled, records updated to the final results, and the history archived for whoever buys from that supplier next. Pay what's due on time (Code 3.3.1), and let the record say what the supplier got right, too (Code 5.3.1).

Friday, February 23. 7:00 AM. The stand, two miles out on the prairie, in a wind that had decided overnight to come from the north. Corinne had the last page of her release plan on a clipboard: twelve names, today's date beside each, promised in April of 2062 when the two teams became one.
Halcyon was five days out, and the stage was flight operations' now.

Keep all twelve through March. If anything comes up with that stage I want the people who built it in the building, not in Limon. He said it on the phone, on speaker, so the whole blockhouse heard it.

Hale's office had a plan for the twelve as well: a ceremony at the Denver office on Monday, with plaques, the families, and Greaves's camera, because they'd earned it and the partners should see who they were.

Corinne had written down what the stand crew wanted, on her legal pad, when she asked them. She tore the page off and put it on the console in front of him. Coffee at the stand. Wendell, if he'll come. Nobody from Denver making a speech.
A. Release them on the date with a company email of thanks, and save the real recognition for September, when the job is properly finished.
B. Release the twelve on the date promised, with open work handed over by name, and thank the stand crew the way they asked to be thanked.
C. Release the twelve on the promised date, and hold Hale's ceremony in Denver for them, with plaques and the families, since they've earned it.
D. Keep all twelve on through March in case the ship needs them, since letting the people who know it go this early is the bigger risk.

By ten every open item on the twelve's lists has a name beside it on somebody else's, and the names have initialed. At eleven Corinne puts the big thermos on the blockhouse console, and it holds coffee for thirty. Wendell comes out with Arlo driving and sits on an upturned cable spool by the door and doesn't make a speech. Nobody asks him to. Hale comes too, without a camera, shakes twelve hands, and asks each of them one question about the stand and listens to the answer. At noon Corinne reads the twelve names off her clipboard with the date beside each, and says that's the last promise on the page. Arlo writes the date on his glove.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Release people on the dates you committed (Code 2.2.3), with their work handed to named owners, and recognize them in a way that fits them. The Guide says recognition works best tailored to the people, and that it doesn't have to be money.

Monday, February 26. 9:00 AM. The ARA's flight rules office had asked every program to send its closing lessons by Friday, March 2, for the rules review on Wednesday, March 14. The form had a box for each lesson, and a box beside it that said PROPOSED ACTION (OPTIONAL).

Quinn had the register sorted by what each lesson touched. The longest pile was the anomaly process. At the top of it was the oldest thing in the program: AR 2207, a criticality 1 anomaly downgraded to criticality 2 eleven days before a review, so that Flight Rule 2.36 printed N/A beside it and never applied.

He knew the rest from page thirteen, and so did the room, because Greaves had run it. In March of 2036 Ruth had written a second line for her rule, that no criticality 1 anomaly could be downgraded without the same three attempts and the same signature, and the agency's lawyers had struck it as too broad, and she'd signed what was left.

Garrett wanted one last lessons session with the leads, on the record, with names, so that nobody could say afterward that the program had covered for anyone. Hale's office wanted a lessons summary for the partners and the press, two pages, about what had gone well, because the next ship's funding would turn on it.
A. Send each lesson to the office that owns the rule it touches, with evidence, a proposed change, and an owner, Rule 2.36's struck line among them.
B. Publish a lessons summary for the partners and the press about what the program did well, since the next ship's funding depends on that story.
C. Hold a last lessons session with the leads and write up what went wrong and who was responsible, so nobody can say the program covered for anyone.
D. Move the program's whole lessons register into the ARA's repository on time, complete and indexed, so the next program can search it when it needs.

It takes the week. Nineteen lessons go out with a proposed action each, to nine offices, and each office's name is on the line with a person's under it. Number one goes to the flight rules office in two sentences. AR 2207 was closed by first downgrading a criticality 1 anomaly to criticality 2, so Rule 2.36 never applied, and the program proposes restoring the line struck in March 2036. Attached are the closure history and a photocopy of a legal pad page from 2036 with the line on it in green, which he'd asked Ruth for on the phone on Tuesday night and which came in Thursday's mail with no note. The office puts it on the docket for March 14 as item one. The proposer's line says S. OKAFOR. The originator's line says R. CALDER, 2036.

Exactly right. Lessons do their work when they change the organization's process assets: route each one to the owner of the rule or procedure it touches, with the evidence and a proposed change, and make sure someone there owns it.

Wednesday, February 28. 4:30 PM. Hale's office had called at noon. The ARA was standing up the program for the next relief ship, for the 2065 window, with a second Breather and a crew of six. It wanted Quinn Abernathy as that program's deputy from Monday, April 2, with the countdown lead's job built in.

The program's closeout ran to March 30. Garrett wanted her kept at Tallgrass through all of it, and then for the bid on the next ship. Hale's office wanted her in April. Delphine Varga had called Sam at two, from the Cape, to say she'd heard, and to say only that Quinn should get to decide, which wasn't usually how it went.

Quinn was at her whiteboard with an eraser in her hand, not erasing anything. Under the box that said TEST TUE JAN 30, the 12 was still there in her small capitals. I heard. Hale's assistant told me before Hale told you, I think by accident. She put the eraser down on the tray. I'd like to finish this one first. That's all I've said to anybody.
A. Keep Quinn through the whole closeout before she goes, since nobody else knows the schedule and the final report needs her more than a new ship.
B. Tell Quinn she ought to take the job, since it's the best thing that could happen to her, and help her write the acceptance to Hale tonight.
C. Ask Quinn what she wants first, then free her for it on a date that works, hand her work to named people, and tell the ARA what she did.
D. Recommend Quinn to the ARA in writing, with her record, and let the agency and Tallgrass work out the timing of the move between themselves.

He asks, and then waits, which takes longer than asking. She wants it. She wants to finish the final report's schedule section first, because it's hers, and she wants Delphine's Thursdays to keep going. They settle on Friday, March 23. Corinne takes the integrated plan's closeout and Peg takes the procurement archive, and both initial it. Then he writes Hale's office a page about her, the plain way: the poll she wouldn't move on from at propulsion, the 12 on the whiteboard, two years of being the one who knew where the schedule was wrong. He shows it to her before he sends it. She reads it with her hands flat on the desk and asks him to take out one adjective. He does.

That's a go. Lead by empowering the person, not deciding for her: ask what she wants, support it, release her on a date that works, hand her work to named owners, and give the next organization an honest account of what she can do.

Saturday, March 10. 10:00 AM. Golden. The garage door was up when he pulled in, which it had never been, and in the middle of the concrete floor, on its tripod, was the telescope. The case was open on the workbench behind it, the foam still holding the shape of what had come out.

Ruth was at the kitchen table where she'd been in January of 2061, with coffee and the green cloth binder, and the green pen lying across the cover. She started before he'd sat down, the way she started pages.

I took it out on the seventeenth, about seven at night. Halcyon went over at 7:14, west to east, low. I'd worked out the pass on a pad. It looked like a star in a hurry. She turned her cup a little on the table. My husband bought it so I could watch the ship go. I watched one go. That's all I wanted from it.

She told him the next part to the binder, not to him. Wendell walked me to my car on the eighteenth, in the lot, after. He said I could ask him now, if I wanted. I said I knew I could, and that I wasn't going to. It wouldn't change what I did on that console. It would only change which of us carried it, and he's carried his half long enough. She drank some of her coffee. He said that was all right. Then he said the wind would come round to the north by noon, and it did.

He waited, because she wasn't finished. You won't get that, about Arizona. Nobody's going to walk you to your car and offer. I'm sorry. I say his name in the mornings now, after Lise's and Kenji's and Roz's. You gave it to me. Four's no harder than three.

He'd brought the envelope. It had been on the counter under his keys since February of 2062, unsealed, with her address on the front in his hand. He put it on the table beside the binder. She opened it, since it wasn't sealed, took out the photocopy, and looked at the third row with the pencil box around it and STILL ASKING beside it in blue ink.

Emmett's row three, she said. He told her Nell had given it to him and that he'd meant to send it, and then hadn't known what he'd be telling her. That I didn't look at it, Ruth said. I know. I've known since September of 2035. She put it inside the front cover of the binder, under the card that said ASK WHY.

The ARA's archivist had written on Wednesday. The program's records were due in the agency's repository on Monday. The board's minutes of December 14 recorded that Member Calder had sent the program manager pages of her console log; could the program include them? A scanning form was attached, with a box for the owner's consent that somebody had already filled in with N/A.
Fourteen pages were in a folder in his bag. The rest were under her hand.
A. Archive only the final report and the decisions, and leave the working files, notes, and pages out, so the next program can find what matters fast.
B. Archive every program record complete, tell the archivist the pages are Ruth's, and ask her, at her own table, what she'd want done with them and with the binder.
C. Scan the fourteen pages he holds into the archive, since the board's minutes already name them and the next program needs them more than a drawer does.
D. Archive every program record complete, leave Ruth's pages out of it entirely, and give all fourteen back to her today, since they're hers and not the ARA's.

The program's records go in complete on Monday: the criteria and the reasoning behind them, the consents and statements, the poll book, the closure history, the run sheets, each with its owner's consent on file where it needs one. He writes the archivist that the pages belong to a private person and aren't the program's to give. Then he asks Ruth. She listens to all of it. No, she says. The agency has the report and the rule. It doesn't get the pages. They were for you. She pushes the binder across the table with two fingers, the way you'd slide a cup to somebody. It's yours. Keep it in the kitchen. Don't frame anything.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Archive the project's records completely for future use, and respect property rights in documents and data (Code 3.3.4): a person's own notes go into an archive only with their consent. Ask the owner, and do what she says.

Monday, March 12. 7:00 AM. The program room had been emptied over the weekend except for Quinn's whiteboard, which she'd asked to keep until the 23rd, and the long table, which nobody could get through the door.
Halcyon was twenty two days out. The Breather was in its module, cold, with six months of cruise and an install between it and anybody breathing what it made.

The final report was due to Hale and the board on Friday, the sixteenth. Quinn had the outline on the screen. Garrett had sent a cover page with a headline on it in bold. Okonkwo's line one, sent on schedule from Mars, said the Breather's benefit hadn't started, because the Breather hadn't.

Hale called at 7:20. Sam, the partners vote on next year's money from this report. It's the story they'll repeat to their own parliaments. I'd like it to be true, and I'd like it to be one they can vote for, and I've been in politics long enough to know those aren't always the same report.
A. Write the report against the baseline, scope, cost, schedule, and quality, with every variance explained, and leave the benefit to Okonkwo's reports.
B. Report each objective against its criteria with the evidence, the risks still open and who owns them, and how much of the benefit is real yet.
C. Report the program as complete and successful on the day it handed over the ship, since what happens to the benefit after that belongs to the station.
D. Write the report as the story of the program, plainly, for the families and partners, and put the tables in an appendix nobody has to read.

It's forty pages, and Quinn's schedule section is the best four of them. Every objective has its criterion beside it and the evidence under it, and where the evidence isn't in yet the report says so and says when it will be. The open risks have owners' names beside them, and none of the names is his. The benefit section is half a page: what the ship was for, what had been delivered toward it, how much of that anybody could measure yet, and Okonkwo's line one with the dates she'll report. Hale reads it twice on Thursday night and calls him at 10:40. It's a hard report to vote for, she says. I'm going to read it to them anyway. It's the one I'd want read to me.

Exactly right. A final report sums up performance against the objectives and their criteria, with evidence, explains variances and open risks with owners, and says how far the benefits have been achieved and when the rest will be known. A project can close before its benefit does; the report says so.

Monday, March 12. 9:40 PM. The kitchen in Aurora. The binder was on the table. He'd set it there Saturday, coming in from Golden, and hadn't opened it. She'd said not to frame anything, and opening it felt close to that.
He opened it at the back. Page fifteen had been folded over once. He unfolded it.
Ruth's console log. Petrel. After. Page 15. oh eight forty one, February 18 2063. watkins. prop took a second. somebody asked.
The page had been blank for twenty six years. The line was green, and it was the only thing on it. 0841. The poll.
He read it until the words came apart into letters, the way he'd read her 0810 line in 2062. He put his thumb under the green line and left it there.
She'd said it was his. He put the binder on the shelf over the coffee maker, beside the sticky note with nine, fourteen, and twenty two on it, and didn't frame anything.

At 10:15 he called Tucson. Ray picked up on the second ring, the way he had for twenty one years. Heard you on the loop, Ray said. Ninety seconds. Longest ninety seconds I ever heard on a loop, and I've heard a few.
Sam read him the line. Ray was quiet so long Sam checked the screen to see if the call had dropped.
You know how you signed this one, Ray said. That's the one you get to keep. Doc's the one you carry. A screen door, and something that creaked when Ray sat on it. The jet doesn't care how you feel.
Doesn't mean I don't get to feel it, Sam said.
Now you're quoting me, Ray said. Go to bed, Okafor.
He'd done most of the last of it the slow way, out loud, with the people who'd have to live with it. It hadn't felt like winning. Ruth would have said that was how you could tell.

Thursday, September 6, 2063. 5:40 AM. One way eight minutes and twenty two seconds. The kitchen in Aurora, with the coffee maker going, the same one, which he'd never replaced, because Grace had bought it and it still worked.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4461. One way, 8 minutes 22 seconds. Margin, 32 days. Hi, Dad. Log ninety eight. Sol 4461. I'm in the C ring airlock. Don't tell the safety officer, he thinks I'm in the galley. The lander came down at 0350 on the old delta, two kilometers out, and the rover's on its way back with all four of them, and the pumps are going on the other side of this door, and in about four minutes I'm going to stop being able to talk. So, quickly. Mom's peppers are flowering. Bay D goes back on the loop tomorrow on the salts you sent. Malik's sign is on Yusra's bunk and it's crooked and nobody's allowed to fix it. You said you were scared, the night before. I played that one more than the burn. And the other thing, about the Cape. She'd have honked the whole way, Dad. I've known that since the bus. I wanted you to know it too. Mine's thirty two. Okonkwo's thirty nine. That's the last time I'm writing those two numbers going down. The light just went green. I can see Yusra's helmet through the little window and she's waving like an idiot. Dad. They're here. Log ninety eight. Ada out.
He watched it three times. The third time he stopped it on her face with the green light behind her, and left it there.

Then he got the gas bill out of the drawer with Grace's reading glasses, soft as cloth now. Minus seventeen, in his own hand from January of 2061. Minus nine. The part number. 12. Under all of it he wrote, in words, the way she'd have said it, plus thirty two. Then he put it under the fruit bowl, face up.
At 6:10 he pressed record, and said hi to her in his own voice, and kept going.

Your ending: Clean Burn. Clean Burn needs AR 2207 reopened, the second test article, the reserve or hot fire 2, and nothing hidden. That's what let Hana call the seat a finding in time. Readiness choices you made: reopened AR 2207 (chapter 2); funded the second test article (chapter 4); held and declared a schedule reserve (chapter 5); funded the autonomy MVP (chapter 7); kept hot fire 2 (chapter 10); had Wendell teach Quinn and the crew in person (chapter 12). Hiding choices: none. This is the right answer path's ending. In the app, your own choices from every chapter decide which of the four you get.
Halcyon readiness in this chapter ended at 100. You closed it the way you'd want it closed.
